newsitem.title: USA: St. Paul seeks sale of risk bonds.
newsitem.headline: St. Paul seeks sale of risk bonds.

text.p: St. Paul Cos Inc hopes to sell a new type of bond this week in the latest attempt by a U.S. insurer to pass some of its insurance risk into the capital markets, sources familiar with the deal said.
The bonds, which are being sold in a private placement, would link an investor's returns to the performance of the company's book of business, the sources said.
That makes the offering somewhat different from other recently-attempted deals, which directly linked returns to catastrophes, sources said. St. Paul declined comment.
Wall Street has attempted several similar deals to securitize insurance risk in recent months, but none so far has been successful.

Indeed, the latest casualty came on Friday when the California Earthquake Authority scrapped its plans to issue $1.5 billion of earthquake risk bonds and instead decided to buy additional reinsurance, the traditional product insurers use to reduce their risk of major losses.
Reinsurance is a form of insurance that insurance companies buy for their own financial protection.

The California Earthquake Authority's governing board scrapped the earthquake risk bond deal because it feared the bonds would be more costly than originally expected and decided to use the more familiar reinsurance contracts.
ACE Ltd and USAA Group also attempted to securitize their risks with similar bond offerings earlier this year.

The St. Paul offering is being made to institutional investors through a special purpose vehicle called Georgetown Re and consists of two tranches, sources said. The one tranche would not put an investor's principal at risk.
But the St. Paul offering does not link an investor's returns directly to catastrophe losses, sources said.

Instead, an investor's returns would depend on how well the book of business was underwritten, much like a quota share reinsurance contract, sources said. The fewer the claims, the better investors' returns. With catastrophe-linked bonds, returns would be cut by frequent or severe catastrophes.
If the St. Paul deal succeeded, it would significantly broaden the potential role of the capital markets in the insurance industry and make the capital markets a major competitor to reinsurers.
Such a development would be welcomed by many primary insurers who currently have no alternatives to the reinsurance market.
"We don't believe there's enough capacity in the reinsurance markets today," Allstate Corp chief financial officer Tom Wilson said.
Wilson said Allstate also was exploring the option of issuing a catastrophe-linked bond, possibly early next year.
Such a bond offering would further reduce Allstate's catastrophe exposure and free it to expand its underwriting, he said.
"Strategically for us it's important to have that capacity available so we can provide that coverage on a pass-through basis to our customers," Wilson said.
However, he said, Allstate is not likely to be a buyer of such bonds in the near future.

"We're a seller of that exposure today, because it impacts the volatility of our earnings; and we've got our (price/earnings ratio) up now, and we'd like it to go up farther, so we're not trying to go the other way," he said.
